title: The Demand at the Sacrifice
subtitle: The Danavas of Shatpura claim a share of Brahmadatta's yajna
story:
"Give us our share in the Yajna. We will drink Soma, and Brahmadatta must give us his daughters."

The demand reached the sacrificial ground of Shatpura in the middle of a year-long rite. It came from Nikumbha and the other Danavas of the city, who assembled on the bank of the sacred river Avarta, a place resorted to by the munis — and they came proud of the boon that made them fearless. They did not frame their words as a request. They claimed a share of the sacrifice, the most valuable of the jewels Brahmadatta possessed, and his daughters, who they had heard were many and beautiful. "If he transgresses this order," they announced, "we will not allow him to celebrate this Yajna. This is our order."

Brahmadatta was a Vajasaneyi Brahmana, a disciple of Yajnavalkya, well-read in the four Vedas and the six Angas, a man of morality — and he answered the Danavas the way his learning taught him. No portion of sacrificial offerings had ever been laid down for them in the Vedas; if they doubted it, they could ask the great munis who sat at the rite. His daughters he would give in marriage to proper bridegrooms, following the same Vedas; that was his resolution. "If you come to terms," he said, "I may give you my entire collection of jewels. If you show your force, I will not give even that — for Devaki's son is my supporter."

The Danavas chose force. They scattered the articles of the sacrifice and began to carry away his daughters.

It happened that Vasudeva and Devaki were themselves at Shatpura, for Brahmadatta was a class-friend and preceptor of Vasudeva, and Krishna's father had come with his wife to protect the rite — just as Indra guards Brihaspati, his own preceptor. Around them sat the greatest of the sages, Vyasa, Yajnavalkya, Sumantu, Jaimini, Dhritiman, Jajali, Devala, and others of firm devotion; and Devaki, by the grace of her son, went among the beggars of the yajna distributing whatever each one asked, in proportion to the wealth of Vasudeva. Such was the household the Danavas had chosen to challenge: the preceptor of Vasudeva, guarded by the mother of Krishna. The sacrifice was rich in food and in gifts — and it was precisely that richness the Danavas meant to tear apart.

When Vasudeva saw the sacrificial articles being robbed by the Asuras, he thought of Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada. And the moment he thought of them, Krishna knew everything. "Proceed, O my son," he said to Pradyumna, "and save the maidens by virtue of your illusive powers. I myself will soon go to Shatpura with the Yadava army."

Pradyumna, ever obedient to his sire, was there within a moment. By his illusive power he took the maidens away, created figures of them to leave before the Daityas, and told Devaki, "Be not afraid." The Danavas, satisfied, carried off the illusory maidens and entered their city in triumph, while Brahmadatta's real daughters were safe. The deception had saved the maidens and bought the sacrifice its peace — for a little while.

The great yajna went on according to proper rites, and its fame spread. All the kings invited by Brahmadatta arrived and encamped near Shatpura: Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the Malava and Tangana kings, Rukmi, Ahvriti, Neela, Narmada, Vinda, Anuvinda, Avantya, Shalya, Shakuni, and other heroic warrior kings besides. The sacrifice that had begun as a year of offerings now wore a ring of armies around it, and every new arrival made the encampment thicker and the air heavier.
reflection: Brahmadatta's defiance rests on one sentence: no share of the offerings was ever laid down for the Asuras in the Vedas, and his daughters will be given to proper bridegrooms, not to force. He stakes everything on the order of the rite and on the name of Devaki's son — and the rescue comes not as a miracle but as a son obeying his father's summons.
next_story_tease: Narada, watching the kings gather around the sacrifice, decided that the assembly needed a conflict — and set out for Nikumbha's house.
hero_scene: Nikumbha and the Danavas scattering the articles of Brahmadatta's sacrifice on the bank of the river Avarta while Devaki looks on, and Pradyumna arriving with his illusive powers to carry the maidens to safety.
